question.text: <math><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub><mover accent="false"><mo>→</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mover><mfenced separators="|"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></mrow></mfenced><mover accent="false"><mo>→</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mover><mn>3</mn></math> monochloro structural isomers for compound <math><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub></math> how many pairs of geometrical isomers are possible?

solution.text:
C5H10→H2/NiX→Cl2/hv3 monochloro structural isomers f(X) must have 3-type of H, so it is n-pentane
Possible structure of C5H10 is
CH3–CH2–CH2–CH=CH2 no G.I
CH3–CH=CH–CH2–CH3 Geometrical Isomer
Only one pair of G.I is possible (cis/trans)
